finding: This check is incomplete and the confidence is low: the run's shared web search allowance ran out partway through, so three of the four classes have no aftermarket parts price (null low ends), each class rests on a single priced parts page, and only two of the three required benchmarks were loaded. On what was verified, the $120 floor of the live range looks about right and the $1,025 ceiling looks high for a single sensor. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks), for one upstream sensor: truck 2016 F-150 3.5L EcoBoost about $128-$327 (0.5-1.0 hr, $68-$167 sensor); economy 2020 Subaru Impreza up to about $551 with a genuine sensor at list ($358.75) and 1.2 hours, low end not built; midsize 2020 Subaru Outback up to about $465 using a dealer selling price of $273.25 (list would be higher), low end not built; luxury 2015 BMW 328i up to about $566 with a genuine sensor at list ($406.30) and 1 hour, low end not built. The one complete low total, $128, is an aftermarket sensor at an online price plus a 0.5 hour warranty time, so $120 is at or just under the supportable floor. The highest total we can build for one sensor is about $566, and the two benchmarks top out at $523 (RepairPal) and $500 (ConsumerAffairs), so nothing found supports $1,025 for one sensor; that figure would fit two sensors replaced together, a dealer rate well above $160 an hour, or a seized sensor needing thread repair, none of which we could put a sourced number on. Treat that as a lead to recheck, not a settled result. How solid the labor times are: two are manufacturer warranty times for the example vehicles, Ford's 0.5 hour (right) and 0.6 hour (left) for the F-150 3.5L EcoBoost including reading the codes, and Subaru's 1.2 hours (front) and 1.0 hour (rear) for the Impreza and Outback. The Subaru time is longer than the general 30 to 60 minute figure, so for those two classes the manufacturer time is the high end and the general figure the low end. The BMW hours are a general statement only; BMW bulletins refer dealers to BMW's own labor system instead of printing a time. Upstream versus downstream: the upstream sensor (an air/fuel ratio or wideband sensor on most newer cars) is the dearer part and the one priced in the classes. Downstream sensors seen: Subaru genuine $232.85 list against $358.75 upstream, with a 1.0 hour rear time against 1.2 front; F-150 genuine rear $138.91 list and aftermarket $34.06-$65.34; BMW $325.06 list against $406.30. A Nissan bulletin (NTB22-007A, 2013-2016 Altima 2.5L and Sentra, rear sensor warranty extension) allows 0.3 hour for the voltage check and 1.3 hours for the readiness drive pattern but prints no separate replacement time. Honda and Acura bulletins that replace an air/fuel sensor together with a catalytic converter (1.3-2.4 hours combined) were not used because the sensor time cannot be separated out.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or code-scan fee (a sensor code can also be caused by an exhaust leak, wiring fault, vacuum leak or a failing catalytic converter, so the sensor is not always the fix), shop supplies and sales tax. V engines have two upstream and two downstream sensors, and a shop may recommend replacing a pair. A sensor seized in the exhaust can add labor or thread repair. Some repairs finish with a drive cycle to reset the emissions readiness monitors, which may be billed as extra time.
